draft/0.1-preface.html.title: 0.1 Preface
draft/0.1-preface.html.description:
It is impossible to understand the state of the modern Empire without understanding the Sages, and the world they hail from. What credible source exist, and the far and few between collected transcriptions of the First Sage tell us that there was advanced civilization on the surface of Oord long before recorded history. Great cities of gleaming metal and glass, and more humans than even this current, most prosperous era. It's not clear exactly what prototypic form of magic this civilization utilized, but at some point a disaster of impossible scale affected their civilization, mutating magic into the form it exists in today. Society fell[1], and humanity was reduced to an inarguably lower state of existence, bands of hunters and scavengers roaming the wastes of civilization. Evidence seems to indicate most early forms of society after the fall revolved around the rare few who had learned to practice Alchemy or Witchcraft. Technology remained scare for centuries, at minimum, with only oral tradition to carry this history of the world that came before. Master-disciple practices of alchemy passed knowledge down, refining methods of materia and ascendence from base principles, only to be lost to happenstance or rivalry. Ritual covens worshipped the first demons, just as likely to harness the fell creatures as to be violently destroyed by them. It was in this dark age that the First Sage ascended, attaining immortality via the first transcendent method of self-alchemy. Over the coming centuries, the accumulating knowledge of the First Sage and his attendant faction pulled humanity out of the dark age, reconstructing some measure of stability. Centuries passed, and it slowly became clear that the ascendance of the First Sage was not simply a matter of simply superior alchemical knowledge and luck, but something deeper. As the written language sprouted anew and generations passed, the First Sage grew distant from their society. They were inarguably above other humans, vastly greater in knowledge, possessing a physical form that could bend tungsten and withstand lava. The affliction that could most harm them was apathy. Eventually, one of the fractured civilizations descending from the First Sage's country produced a second alchemic immortal. For a time, the Second Sage too elevated civilization, codifying the 17 elements of alchemy[2] and constructing many great artifacts to ease the material burden of the still largely-barren landscape of the world... ...Even 3 millennia beyond the era of the Second Sage, only Seven Alchemical Sages exist. Although the Sages are beyond humanity in most ways, it is said their minds are still starkly mortal. They are no more above loneliness than any of us, and their lack of peers only alienates them more. It is for this reason that the Seventh Sage issued the Ascendance Dictate, a comprehensive plan to manipulate the world in an effort to create as many new sages as possible. With the support of the Second and Fifth Sages, the world was largely united under the banner of the New Oordic Alchemic Empire. It is still impossible to tell what makes one capable of refining oneself into an immortal, but commonalities are clear between the Sages that exist. Every Sage was educated, even before they became an immortal. Every Sage lived a relatively stable life, with ascendancies seeming to come closer together as quality of civilization improved, with the obvious exception of the Sixth Era. All ascendancies came in times of peace. Every Sage was a leader or figure of societal importance, though many argue whether this is merely a result of other common qualities. In short, the way to best encourage the qualities that seem to makes a Sage is to ensure thorough education for all in science and alchemy, elevate the standard of life as much as possible, ensure world peace, and provide a path for those who excel in alchemy into government. And of course, make sure there are as many people as possible to give yourself more chances. The darker side of the Dictate is a tale that has been slowly playing out over the ages, the slow ostracization of the Other Magic. Though the Orthopraxy of today barely resembles the demon-calling Witchcraft of ages past, it simply cannot compete in industrial scale against Alchemy. With the release of the Standard Imperia Alchemica, the Seventh Sage's personal self-alchemy guide making it easy to pass the first few and powerful stages of alchemical enhancement, each year there are fewer and fewer practicing or aspiring Praetors. We live in what is most probably the closest thing to a utopia that has ever existed in the history of Oord, and yet- and yet! We would be truly remiss to not acknowledge the cost that this bears on culture and tradition, on important things that maybe shouldn't just be relics of the past. All of what we are is the whim of person of incredible power, and maybe that means something. - Lecture given by Martin Bakal, Tenured Professor of History at Bayfront City College
Next
Some scholars suggest that the sudden new magic described the First Sage also may have come with some form of alteration of the rules of reality. Those who oppose it suggest instead the massive and sudden collapse had to do with some fundamental integration of magic into society: all infrastructure may have relied upon some form of obliviated magic, similar to how most cities today use by centralized alchemical light networks.↩︎
The original treatise was said to only describe 16 elements, with Sulfur only later being reclassified as an element and not a natural phenomenon.↩︎

draft/1.1-leaving-home.html.title: 1.1 Leaving Home
draft/1.1-leaving-home.html.description:
Edward nervously fidgeted with his train ticket. He stood in the grand hall of Ochre Light Station, which served his area of the city.The arched ceilings of what must have been specially formulated stone stood above his head, glistening in a beautiful yellow-orange[1] streaked through with striations of blue veins and patterns like a sunset on an alien planet—and he had heard plenty enough about material formulation from his friends studying industrial alchemy to know what a rarity something like that was. The floor was done in textured green panels, shades of verdant color in subtle peaks and valleys that made one feel as if they were a giant walking on a untouched wilderness landscape.It wasn't that he didn't expect the trip, or wasn't prepared for it. No, he had his rolling suitcase of clothes, and his suitcase of ritual materials too—and he was sure he had packed everything. It was more of.. a yawning sensation in his gut. Like everything was just about to fall away from him. Or maybe even drifting as he stood there now.
It wasn't fear of a new place either. He'd been to so many wilderness preserves with his parents, and if Getschund Brille[2] wasn't an unfamiliar city than what was?
No matter. It would pass, and he knew at least intellectually that he was doing everything he should. The ticket- he glanced downward to read it one more time- yes, the ticket definitely read Bilgeton, and that was where the N3 Bilgeton[3] ruins he was set to investigate were.The sound of wind startled him out of his thoughts, the train appearing through the far windows, slowing down as it reached the station. Edward put the ticket back into his pocket, and rolled his bags up to the line already forming in front of the closet car's doors.Fewer people seemed to be traveling than he thought there would be, only an older man, one couple, and a group of other kids his age. Bilgeton wasn't exactly a tourist destination, but surely one of the other towns on the line had something of note, right? Eh, maybe not. He certainly hadn't heard of anything.
The interior of the car was spacious, decorated in clean white metal and sky-blue highlights, similar to the outside. He quickly found his was to a free table near the end of the car, and rolled his bags underneath. Comfortable seat, too—surprisingly nice fabric for what had to be alchemically generated material[4].Edward sat curled up in the chair, looking over his todo list for the first couple of weeks in Bilgeton. It was evening now, the sun dappling rectangles of soft pink over the metal of the car, light shining from small tubes of lux now ignited above.Check out the furniture situation- couldn't do that yet. Mailbox, Get building supplies, setup Cyrral's Homely Domain—ooh, that one was important—, actually find the ruins, get some groceries- all on wait till he got to Bilgeton. At least he was nearly halfway there, with the train arriving early morning at tenth bell tomorrow. Read History of Northern Inland Kevland Ruins? Uh, no thank you. He was here to test the magic of ruins, not figure out who built them. Check out the Bilgeton pamphlet thingy- yes, that was it.He'd gotten the pamphlet from a guy at the post office, funnily enough. 'Tourist's Guide to Bilgeton, Raskia', with a funny little picture of a mossy rock and fog, and a guy hanging off a wall in a harness. Fog Gulch Bilgeton's most famous landmark, fog gulch is a mist valley only a couple miles outside the center of town. Visit the top of Mt. Verdine for a spectacular view of the entire mist cloud, which lingers perpetually over the area. Dive into the mists below! Strap on a harness and rappel 150 meters down the cliff. Stand on the platform constructed just 20 years ago, and immerse yourself in the droplets of water which give Bilgeton its constant cool temperature, even in the summer months. That could be neat. Maybe he could check that out after he did the home definition ritual, could be nice to see the fog up close. There didn't seem to be anything about the bottom of the valley, but maybe it was all river or something? A Rich Past Bilgeton is one of the most important exporters of Vitae in the greater Lumis area. The special moss that grows in the humid atmosphere of the forest and valley contains a nearly pure mix of Vitae and Tin elements. Bilgeton residents export more than 70 metric tons of moss a year. The first settlers used to grow moss by actually watering it with mechanical spouts, leading to today's affectionate term of 'Daubers' for those who grow moss. Although much of the towns moss is grown in greenhouses for export now, residents today still use the term to celebrate the settler's work.
Interesting stuff, though it was probably nothing very special magically[5]. He would still check it out, of course, but better not to get hopes up. Especially, on second thought, given that they apparently exported this stuff in mass quantity to Lumis and nobody had ever mentioned it at LPC[6].
There was more on the back of the pamphlet, but it seemed to be just be a list of local representatives, and maker's mark[7].No real revelations there, he had already known about the fog from the grant position, but it was nice to know you could see it up close. It did spark some ideas for art projects. He'd have to get Sylis back at the college to mail him a copy of gas containment rituals, but maybe he could do some sort of interactive sculpture.. something where you could go in and out of the fog, full mist to know mist in a single demarcating line? He penned it in at the bottom of the todo list, something to look into later.As the sun was at last fully subsumed by the horizon, Edward folded up his notepad, stretched a little, and settled in to sleep the rest of the train ride.

Ochre, of course↩︎
A city on the Triatic coast famous for it's local language, a rarity when most of the Empire spoke just Anglish↩︎
North quadrant, 3rd instance of ruins found↩︎
The government was famous for making anything and everything out of alchemy, even when it might be better if they hadn't. Case in point: most fabrics on chairs at public institutions felt less woven and more like a wicker basket, though really, there was nothing stopping them from using wooden chairs anyway.↩︎
You did have the rare plant that had both neat alchemical and praxic interactions, but more often than not the systems interacted obliquely.↩︎
Lumic Praxic College, which Edward had studied at for TODO: COLLEGE YEARS NUMBER years.↩︎
First popularized with bespoke alchemical creations, a makers mark is a complex symbol imprinted or etched onto something that indicates the person or group responsible for its creation, without aesthetically marring the object. Town halls provide a catalog service for makers marks, but most tend to be distinct, popular, or local enough not to need the label.↩︎

info_showOrphanNodes.description: Show nodes that are not connected to any other nodes.

info_showAttachments.description: Show attachments like images and PDFs as nodes in the graph.

info_allowGlobalGraph.description: Allow the user to view the global graph of all nodes.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
